subtitle: Through practical coaching, help colleagues examine evidence, consider different perspectives and choose a responsible next step on the equity questions they face.
scope: For leaders, supervisors, team leads and the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant. This course uses practice workplace-development decisions to practice coaching. It is not an IDI assessment, personnel investigation, accommodation determination or replacement for DHS-required analysis and training.
introTranscript: Coaching on equity skills helps staff reason through their own work. The coach can clarify a question, model part of the analysis, offer feedback and help the person try again. The aim is stronger capability, not having the consultant or supervisor complete every task. In this course, a colleague reviews access to a staff development opportunity. You will prepare a coaching purpose, examine evidence and perspectives, compare options, practice communication and follow up. Keep actual personnel information, private reflections and individual IDI results out of practice records. Work at your own pace and use actual policy and authority routes for operational decisions.

lessons.title: Agree on the work skill and coaching purpose
lessons.summary: Set a specific task, clarify the coach’s role and explain what the practice is intended to help the colleague do.
lessons.objective: Define a task-specific equity skill for a practice coaching conversation.
objectives: Define a task-specific equity skill for a practice coaching conversation.
Distinguish coaching, broader mentoring and formal work direction.
Set boundaries that preserve actual policy and personnel processes.
takeaways: Coaching works on a specific skill in a relevant situation.
Clarify the relationship rather than disguising a formal process.
The learner does the reasoning with useful support.
lessons.statement: A clear purpose gives the colleague a task to practice and an honest understanding of the coach’s role.

image.caption: Preparing the purpose makes the conversation more useful than a general request to improve.

intro.heading: Start with what the person needs to do
intro.body:
A practice analyst is asked to review access to a staff development opportunity. Their first note says, “Everyone receives the same invitation, so the process is fair.” A coach could ask them to “be more culturally aware,” but that phrase does not show what to examine. A clearer coaching purpose is to distinguish equal distribution of an invitation from people’s ability to find, understand and act on it, then identify a responsible evidence question.

Explain the task and the relationship. OPM’s general guidance distinguishes coaching focused on immediate skills from mentoring that provides broader career support. That distinction can help the conversation, but it is not a Minnesota procedure. A supervisor’s work direction, an optional consultant conversation and an actual performance process also have different responsibilities. Do not present a required work instruction as an optional chat, or convert a support conversation into an undisclosed employee evaluation. Use the applicable process for actual expectations and records.

Ask what the colleague already understands and where they want help. They may be confident about distributing information but uncertain about comparing participation opportunities. The coach can work from that starting point without assuming an IDI stage, motive or attitude. A person’s question is not proof of resistance or of a particular cultural orientation.

Agree on an observable practice. The learner might name the unsupported inference, identify two relevant barriers and explain what evidence would help. Keep the scope manageable enough for meaningful work. Do not require the coach to solve every policy, resource or authority issue during one conversation.

Set boundaries for the material. Use the practice case rather than actual employee selections or private experiences. Actual accommodation, discrimination, service or safety concerns keep their appropriate routes; a coaching plan does not delay them. No individual IDI result becomes a personnel score or access gate.

Close the preparation with the task, practice, relevant source and next opportunity. This makes the conversation a practical partnership: the coach supports reasoning while the colleague develops their own capacity to do the work.

inThisLesson: Ask about the learner’s starting point.
lessons.keyStatement: Define a practice the learner can demonstrate without creating a hidden personal evaluation.

flashcards.back: Support for a specific skill or immediate work question. The colleague still performs the reasoning.
Broader guidance for career growth. It can complement coaching but does not substitute for actual work direction.
Something the learner can explain or do, such as finding an unsupported inference. It is not a belief score.
A clear statement of what the coach can support and which decisions or concerns use another process.

items.title: Choose a skill rather than a personality goal
items.body: “Identify what equal invitation distribution does and does not show” gives the learner a concrete task. “Become the right kind of person” has no appropriate practice evidence and can invite coercive judgments.

items.title: Clarify authority and records
items.body: The supervisor may direct actual work, while consultant support can develop reasoning. Explain the actual relationship and record expectations rather than implying that every conversation is confidential or optional regardless of context.

items.title: Let the learner identify uncertainty
items.body: A colleague might understand the policy purpose yet need help turning it into a question about the process. Starting there is more productive than repeating an entire course or interpreting uncertainty as opposition.

tabs.label: Coaching
tabs.body: The practice analyst practices distinguishing a sent invitation from actual access to the development opportunity. A coach asks the learner to explain the claim, inspect its basis and try a revised conclusion. This gives immediate feedback on a particular skill rather than asking the coach to supply the entire analysis. The purpose and actual relationship should be clear so the learner knows what is practice and what, if anything, belongs to real work expectations.

tabs.label: Mentoring
tabs.body: A mentoring conversation can address broader development, experience and possible career opportunities. It may be valuable to the analyst without resolving the invitation’s evidence problem in detail. Mentoring does not itself authorize a promotion, select participants or promise an opportunity. OPM’s distinction helps describe the conversation’s purpose; it is general federal guidance rather than a Minnesota process or guaranteed result.

tabs.label: Formal process
tabs.body: Actual work direction, accommodation consideration and a complaint have their own applicable responsibilities. Calling a conversation coaching does not make those responsibilities optional or authorize undisclosed employee evaluation. If a relevant issue arises, retain its proper route while keeping practice separate. This distinction lets support be helpful without concealing the actual purpose or delaying a response the person is entitled to seek.

check.question: Which purpose best fits the practice analyst’s note?
check.correct: Practice distinguishing equal invitations from access to the opportunity, identify a relevant evidence question and clarify the support role.
wrong: Infer the analyst’s IDI stage from the note.
Tell the consultant to complete the analysis instead.
Treat the coaching conversation as a hidden employee evaluation.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The purpose teaches a specific reasoning skill while keeping support and actual authority clear.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A work sentence cannot establish the analyst’s IDI stage; that would turn limited task evidence into an unsupported personal assessment. Having the consultant complete the analysis substitutes another person’s work for the capability the learner needs to develop. A hidden evaluation also misrepresents the relationship and actual records process. Agree on a particular practice and support role, then examine the learner’s own reasoning.

items.text: Explain what equal invitation distribution does not establish.
Identify an evidence question about the opportunity.
Discuss longer-term professional interests with a mentor.
Explore career experience and possible development directions.
Route an actual accommodation request promptly.
Use the applicable procedure for an actual performance expectation.

scenario.context: A practice coach wants to diagnose the analyst’s cultural orientation before discussing the draft.
options: Ask the analyst to explain the draft’s reasoning, agree on a specific practice and keep individual orientation labels out of the coaching record.
Assign a stage based on the sentence.
Require a formal assessment result before access to resources.
responses: The draft can support a practical discussion without becoming an assessment or a gate.
A work sentence does not authorize an individual IDI assessment or personnel label.
Learning access should not depend on an assessment disclosure.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice coaching purpose with a task, skill, role explanation and actual-process boundary.

move.control: The colleague understands the practice and relationship.
move.failure: A vague personality goal replaces a skill.
move.next: Define the task and explain the coach’s role.

lessons.title: Coach the difference between evidence and inference
lessons.summary: Ask questions that expose the unsupported step in a claim and help the learner identify relevant information without inventing a conclusion.
lessons.objective: Identify an unsupported inference in the practice development case.
objectives: Identify an unsupported inference in the practice development case.
Ask a question that connects evidence to the stated result.
Describe missing information without treating it as reassurance or proof of harm.
takeaways: A fact can be accurate while the conclusion drawn from it is unsupported.
Ask what the information actually establishes.
Unknown information needs an evidence question, not an invented answer.
lessons.statement: The coach helps the learner test the reasoning rather than replacing one assumption with another.

image.caption: An evidence question can reveal the missing step between an activity and its result.

intro.heading: Inspect the claim one step at a time
intro.body:
The practice analyst confirms that the invitation was sent to every staff email address. That is a useful fact about distribution. It does not establish that every person could read the invitation, request participation, obtain release time or use the opportunity. The coach can ask, “What does the distribution record answer, and what does it leave open?” This gives the learner a way to examine the inference rather than simply accept a correction.

Separate the source, observation and conclusion. A mailing record answers a distribution question. A review of the actual invitation may reveal an unclear criterion or inaccessible attachment. Relevant participation information could answer other questions, depending on its definition, completeness and permitted use. Do not combine those sources into a universal result without examining their limits.

Ask the learner to identify the missing link. In this case, the claim moves from the same communication being sent to equitable access being established. Possible barriers include an unclear application route, a schedule conflict or a material-access problem. These are questions to investigate, not facts about the actual team. The coach should not announce that a disparity has been proved merely because the original fairness claim is weak.

Choose proportionate information. Inspecting the practice invitation and process may be enough for the practice. Actual employee information needs the appropriate permission, privacy and record handling; more data is not automatically better evidence. Avoid collecting identity, health or personal reflections simply because the question involves equity.

Model how to state uncertainty. “The mailing record shows distribution, but we have not examined whether the route works for different staff situations” is stronger than either “everything is fair” or “the team has discriminated.” It recognizes what is supported and identifies the next question. An actual allegation still follows its relevant process; the coach is not adjudicating it.

Ask the learner to write a revised conclusion themselves. Then compare it with the evidence. This second reasoning step matters: repeating the coach’s wording may be useful initially, but explaining why the claim is limited gives clearer evidence that the skill is developing.

lessons.keyStatement: Correct the unsupported claim without inventing an opposite finding.

flashcards.back: Evidence that an invitation was sent. It does not establish that the opportunity was usable.
A conclusion that goes beyond what the stated information supports.
A question about information that would help examine a specific uncertainty.
A statement that recognizes the supported observation and the unresolved question.

items.title: What does this source answer?
items.body: The mailing record may answer who was included in a distribution list. It does not answer whether the attached document or request route works. This question helps the learner choose evidence suited to the claim.

items.title: What other explanation remains?
items.body: Low participation could reflect opportunity, interest, timing, information or other conditions. A coach should not require a particular explanation before it has support. Identify alternatives and the next relevant information instead.

items.title: How would you revise the claim?
items.body: Let the learner write a conclusion that retains the accurate distribution fact while removing the unsupported fairness claim. Ask them to explain the boundary; that tests reasoning more directly than copying the coach’s sentence.

tabs.label: Known
tabs.body: The mailing record shows that the practice invitation was sent to every staff address. It answers a defined distribution question, which is worth retaining. It does not show whether the attachment was usable, the criteria clear or participation available within a staff member’s actual circumstances. Asking the learner to identify that boundary preserves the useful fact instead of treating a limited source as either complete proof or worthless information.

tabs.label: Unresolved
tabs.body: The invitation’s usability, request route, timing and participation conditions have not been examined. Naming those open questions gives the learner a practical next inquiry. They are possible barriers to investigate, not established facts about a real DHS team. Use proportionate, permitted information rather than gather private identity or health details merely to make the analysis seem more substantial.

tabs.label: Overstated
tabs.body: “Equal sending proves equitable opportunity” moves beyond what the mailing record can establish. The correction is not to declare discrimination without additional evidence. A stronger statement keeps the distribution fact and identifies the access questions still requiring examination. This teaches the learner to match both reassuring and critical conclusions to their actual basis rather than choose whichever statement sounds more committed to equity.

check.question: What should replace “the same invitation proves fair access”?
check.correct: The distribution record shows equal sending; the usability and participation routes remain to be examined.
wrong: Missing feedback proves nobody experienced a barrier.
The analyst’s background explains the error.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This retains the supported fact and names the gap without diagnosing people or making a legal finding.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Rejecting the fairness overclaim does not prove discrimination; the stronger conclusion still needs relevant evidence and its proper process. Missing feedback leaves access unknown rather than confirming nobody faced a barrier. The analyst’s background also does not establish why the error occurred or whether the invitation worked. Keep the supported distribution fact and identify the unexamined participation questions without filling them with personal assumptions.

items.text: All practice email addresses appear in the distribution record.
The reviewed invitation links to an attachment.
Can staff use the attachment and request route?
What relevant barriers affect participation?
Equal sending proves equitable opportunity.
No recorded feedback proves no barrier exists.

lessons.next: Next, examine perspectives without making anyone an identity representative.

scenario.context: The learner corrects the original claim by declaring the opportunity discriminatory, without additional information.
options: Recognize that the original claim needed revision, then ask what evidence supports the new conclusion and what remains uncertain.
Return to the original claim because uncertainty is uncomfortable.
responses: This teaches that both favorable and unfavorable conclusions need support.
Equity language does not make an unsupported conclusion reliable.
A weaker claim does not become valid because the evidence is incomplete.

lessons.transfer: Write an observation, unsupported inference, evidence question and limited conclusion for the practice invitation.

move.control: The learner can explain the evidence boundary.
move.failure: A corrected overclaim is replaced by its unsupported opposite.
move.next: Retain the fact and state the unresolved question.

lessons.title: Help the learner examine perspectives and assumptions
lessons.summary: Make cultural and practical differences part of the reasoning while avoiding stereotypes, compelled disclosure and unsupported individual labels.
lessons.objective: Identify a default assumption in the practice opportunity.
objectives: Identify a default assumption in the practice opportunity.
Prepare a question that can include relevant perspectives without forcing personal disclosure.
Distinguish adapting a practice from stereotyping a person or assigning an IDI orientation.
takeaways: A familiar process can contain assumptions worth examining.
Different perspectives inform the question without becoming stereotypes.
The learner can adapt the work without scoring a person’s cultural development.
lessons.statement: Ask whose experience the process assumes, then seek relevant perspectives through an appropriate and respectful route.

image.caption: A perspective question broadens the analysis beyond the coach’s and learner’s familiar experiences.

intro.heading: Examine the default without inventing the person
intro.body:
The practice development invitation asks people to nominate themselves during a fast public meeting. The analyst considers this straightforward because they find public self-promotion comfortable. A coach can ask, “What does this route assume about how people express interest, and what other ways might support the same purpose?” This question makes the default visible without assigning a cultural trait to any colleague.

DHS’s Equity Policy describes intercultural competence as shifting perspective and adapting behavior across cultural differences and commonalities. In coaching, the skill can be practiced by examining the learner’s own assumption, considering another plausible perspective and developing a workable alternative. It does not require the coach to determine the learner’s individual position on an IDI continuum. Formal assessment and individual results remain separate; a practice response does not become an employee label.

Consider more than one explanation. A person may avoid public nomination because of preference, culture, disability access, a power relationship, schedule or uncertainty about the selection criteria. Those are possibilities, not diagnoses. Ask relevant questions about the process rather than assigning a reason from identity, silence or appearance.

Meaningful input needs an appropriate route. A practice exercise can use prepared perspectives. Actual engagement should explain purpose, influence and how information will be used; it should not require private disclosure to make a concern legitimate. One person’s experience can reveal a useful issue but cannot represent an entire group or establish how common the issue is.

Ask the learner to compare an alternative such as a clear written expression-of-interest route alongside an appropriate discussion opportunity. The purpose is to let people communicate interest through a usable process, not to assume one format suits everyone or bypass accommodation requirements. The actual selection criteria and authority still need review.

The coach can model curiosity by naming their own default: “I initially assumed public nomination was easy because it works for me.” Then return the work to the learner. Ask them to identify the assumption, seek appropriate input and explain a possible adaptation with its limits. This develops perspective-taking as a practical skill rather than a personal ranking.

inThisLesson: Explain a possible adaptation and its limits.
lessons.keyStatement: An adaptation begins with a question about the practice, not a stereotype about a person.

flashcards.back: A familiar way of doing something treated as universally workable, such as public self-nomination.
Examining how another experience may change the meaning or burden of a practice. It does not require agreement on every issue.
An appropriate change in communication or practice that responds to relevant differences while retaining the task’s requirements.
Coaching comments and exercises do not authorize an IDI score, hidden label or personnel ranking.

items.title: Ask about the process rather than an identity
items.body: “How can staff express interest?” is an appropriate task question. “Do people from that group dislike speaking?” assumes a trait and can distort both the evidence and the relationship. Keep the analysis open to individual and contextual differences.

items.title: Do not turn one account into the whole picture
items.body: A voluntary perspective may expose an overlooked burden. It does not establish prevalence or speak for every colleague. Ask what other information is relevant and preserve the account’s limits.

items.title: Adapt without creating a shortcut around requirements
items.body: A written route may reduce one barrier while creating others. Examine clarity, access, timing and actual selection rules. A useful option is not automatically a final decision or an approved accommodation.

tabs.label: Personal reflection
tabs.body: The learner notices that public self-nomination feels natural because they are comfortable announcing interest. That private insight can reveal a default without becoming an employee record or a diagnosis of cultural orientation. It is worth retaining even before a proposed process changes. Reflection should open a relevant question about other meanings and situations, not turn the learner’s own experience into a universal account.

tabs.label: Process inquiry
tabs.body: Ask how the nomination route works for relevant staff situations, what its purpose is and whose appropriate input could help examine it. Public silence may involve preference, culturally learned meanings, timing, power or another condition; none is established from identity alone. A useful inquiry explains its scope and possible influence without demanding personal disclosure or making one colleague responsible for representing an entire group.

tabs.label: Practical adaptation
tabs.body: A written expression-of-interest route might provide preparation time while preserving the purpose of communicating interest. The learner should explain that rationale and examine accessibility, criteria, administration and actual authority. Offering an alternative is not proof it works for everyone or that a cultural interpretation is correct. The proposed change becomes stronger when the explanation connects a relevant perspective to a specific method and keeps unexamined effects visible.

check.question: Which question best supports intercultural coaching in the practice nomination case?
check.correct: What does public self-nomination assume, what perspectives are missing and what appropriate alternative could support the same purpose?
wrong: Which identity group is naturally quiet?
What IDI stage does each response reveal?
Can the person disclose a painful experience to prove the issue matters?
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The question examines the default and possible adaptation without stereotyping or making disclosure a requirement.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Assigning natural quietness to an identity group replaces inquiry with a stereotype. A nomination response cannot locate anyone on the IDI continuum or justify a personal employee label. Requiring a painful disclosure also makes testimony a gate to considering the issue and imposes an unnecessary burden. Examine the learner’s default and relevant perspectives through appropriate input, then explain a possible adaptation without diagnosing a person or group.

items.text: What does the public route assume about expressing interest?
Which relevant experiences have not been considered?
Offer a clear written interest route for review.
Provide usable information before the discussion.
A quiet participant must be at a particular IDI stage.
Everyone sharing an identity prefers the same communication format.

lessons.next: Next, compare options and coach a recommendation that states its tradeoffs.

scenario.context: The learner recommends a written route because “people from that community cannot self-promote.”
scenario.prompt: What feedback would strengthen the recommendation?
options: Remove the stereotype, explain the process assumption and identify relevant input and access questions for the proposed route.
Keep the stereotype because the option seems helpful.
Reject all adaptations so everyone must act the same way.
responses: The option can be examined on its purpose and evidence without assigning a group trait.
A potentially useful option does not validate the explanation used to justify it.
Treating one route as universal can preserve the original assumption.

lessons.transfer: Name one personal default in a practice process, an appropriate perspective question and an adaptation to examine.

move.control: The learner examines assumptions and alternatives.
move.failure: A possible cultural difference becomes a fixed trait or employee label.
move.next: Ask about the process, relevant perspectives and limits.

lessons.title: Coach a recommendation with alternatives and tradeoffs
lessons.summary: Help the learner compare practical options, explain their evidence and identify who can decide, rather than treating the first idea as the answer.
lessons.objective: Compare two options for the practice development route.
objectives: Compare two options for the practice development route.
Explain a potential benefit, burden and unresolved question for each option.
Prepare a conditional recommendation with the actual authority boundary visible.
takeaways: Compare options against the same relevant questions.
A useful idea can have burdens or unresolved requirements.
A recommendation explains its reasoning and decision boundary.
lessons.statement: The learner should be able to explain why an option is recommended, what it may change and what remains uncertain.

image.caption: Comparing options makes a recommendation easier to examine and improve.

intro.heading: Ask for reasoning beyond the preferred option
intro.body:
The practice analyst proposes a written interest form instead of public self-nomination. The idea may give staff time to consider the opportunity, but it could also create an inaccessible form or unnecessary burden. The coach should help the learner compare options rather than approve the first alternative because it sounds inclusive.

Choose common questions: how clearly does the route explain the opportunity and criteria, how can people express interest, what access and time burdens arise, who reviews the information and what requirements apply? Compare the existing public route, the proposed written route and, if useful, a combined approach. Do not assume that adding routes is cost-free or that one format meets everyone’s needs.

Ask the learner to distinguish expected effects from supported observations. A written route may offer preparation time; that is a plausible reason to examine it, not proof that it will change participation. A tested access problem in the proposed form would be evidence about that artifact, not a judgment of staff preferences. Record the next relevant question instead of filling an unknown with a confident number.

Include authority and resources. Who can change the process? What information and review are needed? Which staff will administer a new route, and can they do so without adding hidden work? The coach can support the reasoning but should not create an unapproved commitment or treat participation in the conversation as consent.

Ask for a conditional recommendation. For example, prepare a clear written interest route for the actual review, retain an appropriate question opportunity and verify the criteria, access and administration before use. This is a proposed next step, not a determination about real selection outcomes. If the proposal requires formal equity analysis, its applicable tools and consultation remain.

The coach’s feedback should explain which comparison is strong and where an option has not been examined. Then let the learner revise the recommendation. This makes alternatives and tradeoffs part of their capability instead of having the coach supply a preferred answer.

inThisLesson: Keep expected effects separate from findings.
State the recommendation and actual decision route.
lessons.keyStatement: A stronger recommendation makes its alternatives and limits visible.

flashcards.back: A relevant question applied consistently to each option.
A benefit and burden that must be examined together rather than hiding one to promote an option.
A plausible outcome that has not yet been demonstrated.
A reasoned proposed next step that states the evidence, remaining questions and actual authority.

items.title: Use the same questions
items.body: If the written route is judged for accessibility but the public route is judged only for convenience, the comparison is uneven. Examine both for relevant access, clarity, burden and administration. Different findings can follow from a consistent comparison.

items.title: Inspect the hidden work
items.body: A new route may require staff to explain criteria, manage responses and handle questions. Identify who can do that work and what capacity is available. Calling an option simple does not remove its implementation needs.

items.title: Make the recommendation examinable
items.body: State the purpose, reasoning and next review rather than “this is the equitable option.” A conditional recommendation gives decision makers something to inspect and allows the learner to update it when evidence changes.

tabs.label: Public nomination
tabs.body: A public nomination can allow immediate questions and interaction, but its pace and visibility may shape how people express interest. Examine preparation, applicable access needs and power relationships rather than assume silence shows unwillingness. Its usefulness depends on the task and actual process. Keeping this route should be a considered choice, not a claim that everyone ought to be comfortable with the leader’s preferred method.

tabs.label: Written interest
tabs.body: A written route can give someone time to prepare an expression of interest and make criteria available for review. It can also create an inaccessible form, unexplained field or uncertain return path. Examine the complete task, appropriate information handling and a question route. The learner’s recommendation needs these distinctions so a potentially useful idea does not become automatic approval merely because it is quieter than public nomination.

tabs.label: Combined route
tabs.body: Offering both routes may allow different ways to express interest, but the options need consistent criteria, a clear review process and realistic administration. Otherwise, one route may receive different treatment or add hidden work to staff. Compare how the combined arrangement serves the actual purpose and what remains unresolved. More options are not automatically more equitable, and the coach cannot create an unapproved commitment by praising the proposal.

check.question: Which recommendation shows the strongest reasoning?
check.correct: Prepare a written route for actual review, explaining its purpose, comparison, access and administration questions, and the role that can decide.
wrong: Declare the written route universally equitable.
Choose the option requiring the least leader time regardless of staff burden.
Ask the consultant to select real participants.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This makes the option’s value and remaining work visible while preserving the actual decision process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A written route is not universally equitable simply because it is different; its access, criteria and administration still matter. Selecting solely for leader convenience may move work or barriers to staff without examining them. Asking the consultant to select actual participants also assumes authority that coaching does not provide. Compare the relevant effects and unresolved requirements, then prepare a recommendation through the actual decision role.

items.text: Can each route be used through relevant access processes?
Who administers the additional route?
Prepare the written route for authorized review.
Verify the criteria and question path before use.
The new form guarantees equitable participation.
A combined route has no implementation burden.

lessons.next: Next, give feedback and practice a conversation that invites reasoning without losing accountability.

scenario.context: The learner says the new form is automatically best and leaves out administration and access questions.
options: Recognize the preparation-time rationale, ask for a consistent comparison and have the learner revise the recommendation with unresolved questions and authority.
Approve it because a new option sounds positive.
Reject it without explaining the missing reasoning.
responses: This preserves a useful idea while teaching the comparison needed for a stronger recommendation.
Positive intent does not settle burdens or requirements.
An unexplained rejection gives the learner little basis for improving the work.

lessons.transfer: Compare two practice options using clarity, access, burden, administration and authority; write a conditional next step.

move.control: The learner can explain the option and its limits.
move.failure: A preferred idea is treated as proven or automatically authorized.
move.next: Compare the alternatives and state the next review.

lessons.title: Practice the coaching conversation
lessons.summary: Use specific feedback, invite the learner’s reasoning and respond to actual concerns through the right route.
lessons.objective: Prepare feedback that identifies a strength and a specific reasoning gap.
objectives: Prepare feedback that identifies a strength and a specific reasoning gap.
Respond respectfully when a learner explains or challenges the feedback.
Recognize an actual accommodation or complaint matter that must not wait for coaching.
takeaways: Specific feedback teaches the next attempt.
A respectful challenge can clarify the work.
Actual accommodation and concern routes remain active.
lessons.statement: A coach can be clear about the task while remaining open to the colleague’s explanation.

image.caption: A practice conversation helps the coach examine their own assumptions as well as the learner’s work.

intro.heading: Give feedback that can be used
intro.body:
The practice learner compares options well but writes that the current process is unfair because some colleagues did not speak at the meeting. The coach can recognize the useful comparison and identify the unsupported inference: silence does not by itself explain a person’s access, interest or experience. Ask what the learner would need to know and invite a revised statement.

Prepare feedback around the work. Identify the passage, explain the gap and offer a practice task. “Your options identify different routes; the conclusion about silence needs a relevant question rather than a personal assumption” is more useful than “you are not inclusive.” A clear consequence helps the learner understand why the reasoning matters: the current claim could misrepresent people and lead the team to address the wrong barrier. That is a risk to examine, not a proven outcome.

Let the colleague respond. They may have received relevant information not included in the practice draft, or they may disagree about the interpretation. Ask about the source and scope rather than treating a challenge as defiance. Respectful disagreement and professional supervision are distinct from disrespectful conduct under MMB 1432. Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures. That duty follows an actual manager or supervisor role, not every coaching relationship; employees are strongly encouraged to report. Sexual-harassment matters use their applicable separate policy. Do not make a practice conversation a gate to the relevant response.

Likewise, coaching does not delay an accommodation request. Under MMB 1433, an initial request can be oral, written or electronic and does not require special words. A supervisor promptly routes the request and informs the person of the decision maker; supervisors and managers do not request medical documentation. A person should not have to complete another coaching exercise before that process begins.

Practice the response in practice roles. The coach states the specific observation, the learner explains their reasoning, and both identify a relevant next attempt. Do not rehearse an actual employee’s private case in the group. Use the exercise to improve clarity and inquiry, not to adjudicate a real concern or evaluate personal loyalty.

Close with the revised claim and next task. The conversation should leave the colleague knowing what to retain, what to examine and where an actual issue goes.

inThisLesson: Keep actual requests and concerns separate.
Agree on a useful next attempt.
lessons.keyStatement: Clear feedback and respectful inquiry can work together without delaying a required response.

flashcards.back: An identifiable feature of the work that the learner and coach can examine.
The unsupported step that needs a question, evidence or revision.
A disagreement about the task or interpretation that remains professional. It is not automatically misconduct.
The actual process begins from a qualifying request without requiring special words or another coaching attempt.

items.title: When the learner explains new information
items.body: Ask what the information shows, where it comes from and whether it can appropriately support the claim. Do not accept it unexamined, but do not ignore it merely because it changes the coach’s interpretation.

items.title: When the learner disagrees
items.body: Return to the task and evidence: which step in the reasoning is in dispute? Professional disagreement can improve analysis. A coach should not demand agreement as evidence of equity commitment.

items.title: When an actual request appears
items.body: Recognize and use the relevant route promptly. An accommodation request does not depend on knowing the correct phrase. Do not ask for medical records or keep the request in the learning session while deciding whether the person deserves support.

tabs.label: Retain
tabs.body: The draft usefully compares public and written routes and identifies administration questions. Name that strength so the learner knows which reasoning to retain. A precise acknowledgment differs from praising the whole conclusion: it does not approve the unsupported inference about silence. Keeping useful parts makes revision more instructive than requiring the learner to abandon an idea without understanding what was sound.

tabs.label: Examine
tabs.body: The claim that silence proves unfairness leaves out why people did not nominate themselves and whether the route worked in their actual circumstances. Point to that missing link and ask what information could examine it. Do not replace one unsupported explanation with another. The consequence matters: an assumed reason could direct the proposed repair toward a barrier the evidence has not established.

tabs.label: Try again
tabs.body: Ask the learner to write a scoped conclusion that retains the route comparison and states the participation question still open. Let them explain why the revised statement fits the available source. That attempt gives feedback a real purpose and shows the learner’s reasoning more clearly than copying the coach’s wording. Actual concerns still use their proper procedures; a practice revision is not a prerequisite for support or reporting.

check.question: During actual coaching, a colleague asks for a change because of a medical condition. What should the supervisor do?
check.correct: Use the applicable prompt accommodation route without waiting for further coaching, and leave any appropriate medical-document request to the ADA coordinator.
wrong: Require the phrase reasonable accommodation before acting.
Ask the employee for their medical records.
Finish several practice activities before forwarding the request.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. MMB 1433 recognizes requests without special words and assigns prompt routing and medical-document responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Policy 1433 recognizes an initial request without a special phrase, so requiring those words can create an improper gate. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation, and agencies do not request or accept medical records for this accommodation process; appropriate requests belong to the agency ADA Coordinator. Finishing practice activities first also delays the prompt forwarding and decision-maker notice. Use the actual procedure rather than make coaching a condition of support.

items.text: Ask what supports a draft’s claim about silence.
Invite an explanation of a disputed comparison.
Promptly forward a request for a change because of a medical condition.
Consult the ADA coordinator about the appropriate process.
Use the relevant route for an actual harassment concern.
Do not adjudicate a complaint in the practice exercise.

lessons.next: Next, follow up on the learner’s work without creating a hidden equity ranking.

scenario.context: A practice coach interprets the learner’s disagreement as proof of resistance and writes a cultural-orientation label.
options: Remove the unsupported label, examine the specific disagreement and use appropriate task feedback and actual processes where needed.
Keep the label as a coaching shortcut.
Require the learner to agree before accessing resources.
responses: This returns the conversation to evidence and preserves the personal-information boundary.
A shortcut does not make an inferred orientation valid or appropriate for personnel records.
Agreement is not the access condition or a measure of developed skill.

lessons.transfer: Rehearse a practice feedback exchange with a strength, gap, learner explanation and next attempt; identify the boundary for actual requests.

move.control: The learner receives useful feedback and knows the actual routes.
move.failure: Disagreement is labeled or a real request is delayed.
move.next: Return to the evidence and activate the relevant process.

lessons.title: Review growing capability and reduce unnecessary dependence
lessons.summary: Examine the learner’s own reasoning over time, adjust support and keep conclusions specific to the work reviewed.
lessons.objective: Identify evidence of a specific coached skill in a second practice attempt.
objectives: Identify evidence of a specific coached skill in a second practice attempt.
Choose an appropriate support adjustment without declaring universal competence.
Prepare follow-up that keeps missing information and actual authority visible.
takeaways: Review the learner’s own work rather than the coach’s finished product.
Reduce unnecessary support when the specific task evidence supports it.
A work example does not establish a personal stage or universal skill.
lessons.statement: The aim is growing capability to examine equity questions independently, with support available when it helps.

image.caption: A second attempt can show which reasoning is clearer and what still needs guidance.

intro.heading: Follow the skill, not a personal ranking
intro.body:
In the practice follow-up, the learner now separates the distribution fact from the access question, examines public and written interest routes and states what the actual decision process must review. This is useful evidence about the reasoning in the reviewed task. The coach can recognize that progress without declaring the person fully competent in every equity situation or assigning an IDI stage.

Examine the learner’s own work. A final draft that the coach rewrote does not establish independent skill. Ask the learner to explain the comparison and try a related practice task. For example, how would the same questions apply to onboarding information rather than a development opportunity? A transfer attempt can reveal which reasoning is understood and where more support would help.

Adjust the support proportionately. The coach might move from a worked example to guiding questions, then to feedback on the learner’s prepared analysis. This is a suggested learning pattern, not a mandatory sequence or a gate to resources. Staff can still ask for consultant guidance, and the relevant formal process remains even when the person can reason independently.

Keep the follow-up specific. Describe which skill appeared in the reviewed examples, which question remains and what next practice is useful. Do not infer beliefs, loyalty, cultural identity or individual orientation from comments or willingness to agree. Actual job expectations and records use their proper processes; the coaching exercise does not create a hidden personnel score.

Missing follow-up information remains unknown. A person who has not returned a draft has not automatically failed to learn or demonstrated success. Ask about the feasible opportunity, access and task conditions before interpreting the absence. Likewise, a better practice answer does not prove a real service result or eliminate a disparity.

Close with a plan the learner can use: prepare the next relevant question, identify the source and authority, use available guidance when needed and review what the actual work shows. The consultant’s leadership and knowledge remain important while staff develop their own capacity. This balances support with the program’s purpose of enabling equity practice throughout DHS.

inThisLesson: Adjust support to the observed need.
Limit claims and preserve actual processes.
lessons.keyStatement: Describe the skill demonstrated and the next support need without labeling the person.

flashcards.back: Work the learner prepares and can explain, with its support conditions clear.
A change in coaching that responds to the specific demonstrated skill or need. It is not a status ranking.
A related task that asks whether the learner can use the reasoning in another relevant situation.
What the reviewed work does not establish, including universal competence, real-world impact or individual orientation.

accordion.heading: Follow up without creating dependence or overclaims

items.title: Let the learner explain the next case
items.body: Moving the question from development to onboarding can show whether the learner understands the distinction between sending information and usable access. Keep the case practice and the expected skill clear. Do not use it to diagnose personal development.

items.title: Change support rather than remove it as a reward
items.body: More independent preparation can be appropriate when the work shows the reasoning is clear. Guidance remains available for complex or unfamiliar questions; asking for help is not proof that the learner has regressed.

items.title: Name what remains unknown
items.body: No returned draft may reflect workload, access or an unclear task. A stronger answer may reflect practice but not yet actual implementation. Keeping those limits visible helps the coach choose a useful next step rather than an unsupported judgment.

tabs.label: Specific progress
tabs.body: The reviewed second attempt distinguishes distribution from access and compares the routes with relevant burdens. That supports a specific progress claim about the learner’s reasoning in this task. It does not establish an individual IDI stage, every future capability or actual equitable selection. Precise recognition gives the learner something useful to build on without turning one draft into a personal rank.

tabs.label: Remaining question
tabs.body: The learner has not yet applied the comparison to another task, and the real proposal has not completed its process. These are different open questions: transfer of a skill and actual operational authority or effect. Keep them separate rather than infer success or failure from an absent draft. A private insight can still matter while broader capability and work outcomes remain unexamined.

tabs.label: Next support
tabs.body: A related practice onboarding task can offer an opportunity to explain and use the same reasoning with new facts. The coach can then provide targeted feedback and allow more independent preparation. This is a suggested support pattern, not a completion gate or a reason to remove every future resource. Actual analysis and decision processes remain even when the learner can prepare a thoughtful recommendation without continuous coaching.

check.question: What does the improved practice second attempt establish?
check.correct: Specific reasoning improved in the reviewed work; broader capability and actual outcomes need their own evidence.
wrong: The learner has reached an advanced IDI stage.
Every future equity question can be handled without support.
The real development process has become equitable.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The claim recognizes progress without turning a task example into a personal assessment or an operational result.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The improved practice draft cannot establish a personal IDI stage. It also cannot show that every future equity question requires no support, because a new task may involve different evidence or authority. A practice answer does not itself make the actual development process equitable or complete its decision requirements. Recognize the specific reviewed reasoning and keep related practice, optional guidance and actual work evidence available.

items.text: The learner can explain the options in the reviewed draft.
The second attempt states the missing evidence clearly.
Ask for a related practice onboarding question.
Offer targeted feedback when a new complexity appears.
A correct answer proves an individual IDI stage.
No returned draft proves the learner has no equity commitment.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare, practice and follow up on a specific coaching task.

scenario.context: The learner’s second draft is stronger, and the coach wants to remove all future consultant support.
scenario.prompt: What is the better next step?
options: Recognize the specific progress, allow more independent preparation and keep targeted support and actual formal routes available.
End all support because the course is complete.
Keep doing the entire analysis for the learner despite the progress.
responses: This supports independence without pretending that every future question is the same or removing required processes.
Completion and one draft do not eliminate new complexity or the usefulness of guidance.
Continued substitution can prevent staff from developing and using their own capability.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice follow-up note with demonstrated reasoning, its limit, a related practice and a targeted support plan.

move.control: Support responds to the learner’s demonstrated work.
move.failure: The coach either takes over indefinitely or declares universal mastery.
move.next: Describe specific progress and offer the next appropriate opportunity.

jobAid.subtitle: Coach a specific equity skill while the colleague retains responsibility for the work.
remember: Use practice or appropriately cleared material.
No inferred IDI orientations, personal belief scores or hidden employee rankings.
Actual formal analysis, accommodation, complaint and personnel processes remain separate.

Managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follow agency procedures; coaching is not a reporting prerequisite.

sections.heading: Prepare
items: Name the work task and observable skill.
Clarify whether the conversation is coaching, mentoring or actual work direction.
Ask what the learner knows and where support would help.
Explain the material, records and authority boundaries.

sections.heading: Coach the reasoning
items: Ask what the source establishes and what remains open.
Identify the default assumption without stereotyping people.
Compare alternatives with the same relevant questions.
Give a specific strength, gap and supported next attempt.

sections.heading: Follow through
items: Let the learner prepare and explain the next work.
Reduce unnecessary substitution while guidance remains available.
Describe only what the reviewed task shows.
Keep missing information visible and use the relevant actual decision route.
